samples.text:
Every day, a huge amount of food is thrown away by families, restaurants and supermarkets. This is a serious problem because many people in the world do not have enough to eat. This essay will discuss the causes of food waste and what can be done to reduce it.

There are some reasons why people waste food. The first reason is that many families buy more food than they need. When they go shopping, they see special offers like buy one get one free, so they buy a lot and later the food go bad in the fridge. Another reason is that people are confused about the date on the food packet. They think the food is dangerous after the date, so they throw it even if it is still good to eat. In restaurants, the portions are often too big, and customers cannot finish their meal. Also, supermarkets throw away fruit and vegetables which do not look perfect, because customers do not want to buy them.

There are several ways to reduce this problem. Firstly, people should plan their meals before shopping and make a list, so they only buy what they really need. Secondly, the government could make the labels more clear and explain the difference between use by and best before. Thirdly, supermarkets and restaurants should give their extra food to charities or food banks instead to throw it away. Some countries already have laws about this and it is very useful.

In conclusion, food waste is caused by buying too much, confusion about dates and big portions in restaurants. If families, business and government all take action, the amount of food waste can be reduced a lot.
samples.why: Causes and solutions both addressed · ideas relevant but explained simply · repetitive, mechanical linking · adequate everyday vocabulary · several errors in agreement, comparatives and word choice that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
A significant proportion of the food produced around the world never reaches anyone's plate, being discarded instead by households, restaurants and retailers. This essay will outline the main reasons for this waste and suggest how it could be reduced.

At the household level, the key cause is poor planning combined with the relatively low cost of food in many countries. Shoppers often buy more than they need, particularly when tempted by multi-buy promotions, and perishable items such as bread and salad are then forgotten until they have spoiled. Confusion over date labels makes the situation worse, as many consumers treat a best-before date as a strict deadline and throw away food that is perfectly safe. In the commercial sector, the causes are somewhat different. Restaurants frequently serve portions that are larger than customers can eat, while supermarkets reject large quantities of fruit and vegetables for cosmetic reasons and discard stock once it passes its display date.

Reducing this waste requires action from several directions. Firstly, clearer labelling would make a considerable difference; if packaging only showed a use-by date where there is a genuine safety risk, consumers would throw away far less. Public campaigns that teaches simple habits, such as checking the fridge before shopping and freezing leftovers, could also change behaviour over time. For businesses, governments could introduce regulations requiring large supermarkets to donate unsold but edible food to charities rather than sending it to landfill. Restaurants, meanwhile, could offer smaller portions at lower prices and encourage diners to take leftovers home.

In conclusion, food waste results mainly from overbuying, misunderstanding of labels and commercial practices that put appearance and convenience before efficiency. A mixture of better information, changes in consumer habits and sensible regulation could reduce it substantially.
samples.why: Clear focus on causes and solutions · household and commercial causes distinguished and supported · logical paragraphing with good referencing · less common vocabulary (perishable, multi-buy promotions) · one minor agreement slip.

samples.text:
Despite widespread concern about food insecurity, vast quantities of edible food are discarded daily in homes, restaurants and supermarkets. The causes differ across these settings, but in each case waste stems from habits and systems that prioritise convenience over efficiency, and it can be reduced considerably through a mix of education, regulation and incentives.

In households, waste is largely a product of how people shop and store food. Relatively low prices in wealthier countries mean that discarding a half-used loaf carries little financial sting, while bulk promotions encourage people to buy more than they can realistically consume before it spoils. Misleading date labels compound the problem: many consumers fail to distinguish between a use-by date, which concerns safety, and a best-before date, which relates only to quality, and so throw away food that is still perfectly edible. The commercial sector has its own drivers. Supermarkets impose strict cosmetic standards that exclude misshapen produce before it even reaches the shelves, and they routinely overstock to avoid empty displays. Restaurants, for their part, often serve generous portions as a marker of value, much of which is left uneaten.

Tackling these causes calls for measures tailored to each. Simplifying date labelling, and removing best-before dates from items such as fresh fruit altogether, would prevent a great deal of unnecessary disposal at home, particularly if accompanied by public campaigns on meal planning and storage. For retailers, legislation obliging large stores to redistribute surplus edible food to charities has proved workable in several countries and could be adopted more widely. Supermarkets could also be encouraged to sell imperfect produce at a discount, and restaurants to offer flexible portion sizes.

In conclusion, food waste arises from overbuying, confusing labels and commercial practices that value appearance and abundance. Clearer information, redistribution laws and changes to retail and catering practice together offer a realistic path to reducing it.
samples.why: Causes and solutions fully developed and matched to each other · skilful organisation and cohesion · precise vocabulary (compound the problem, misshapen produce, redistribute surplus) · wide range of accurate complex structures.
